content.p: Nearly three decades after a six-year-old girl was found dead in the basement of her family's home in Boulder, Colorado, the question of who killed JonBenét Ramsey has no answer. No one has been charged. The first suspects, her parents, were named publicly as under suspicion for years, and in 2008 the local district attorney formally cleared them and their son after new DNA tests found the profile of an unidentified man on the child's clothing. As of Boulder police's December 2021 release, the profiles had not produced a hit in the national CODIS database. The case is open, and Boulder police describe it as a priority.

What remains in the public record is a set of widely reported facts, a set of contested readings of the same evidence, and a long argument about whether the police, the prosecutors or the press did the most damage in the early days.

On 25 December 1996, JonBenét, her brother Burke and their parents, John and Patsy Ramsey, came home from Christmas dinner at the house of a family friend. According to CNN, Patsy Ramsey put her daughter to bed. The next morning Patsy found a long, rambling note on the spiral staircase and called 911, begging for help.

The note was written on paper that appeared to come from a notepad in the house. Its demand was a specific sum, which CNN, CBS News and Fox News give as $118,000, the same amount as a bonus John Ramsey had received as president of Access Graphics. Law Week Colorado gives the figure as $188,000. Different outlets also describe the note as two and a half or three pages long. More than 28 years on, CNN observed, it is still not clear why someone would write a ransom note describing a kidnapping and then leave the child's body inside the house.

For several hours nobody found JonBenét. CNN reported that family friends came and went freely from the house that day, which led critics to question whether the scene had been contaminated. Law Week Colorado, citing court records, said the police did not ask to interview the Ramseys separately that day and that most of the house was not sealed off. Her father found her body in the basement later that day. According to the same court records, her mouth was covered with duct tape, a cord was around her neck attached to a wooden garrote, and her hands were bound above her head. She was covered with a blanket.

The autopsy found she had died of asphyxia by strangulation associated with craniocerebral trauma. CNN said the skull fracture measured 8.5 inches, and a CNN timeline records that reports of the fracture surfaced on 4 January 1997. Court documents cited by CNN indicate she had also been sexually assaulted.

Because John, Patsy and nine-year-old Burke were the only people known to be in the house, suspicion fell on the family almost at once. CBS News noted that the presence of the parents in the home fueled speculation that one of them had written the note. In 1997 the then Boulder County District Attorney, Alex Hunter, said, according to CBS News, that the parents were under an "umbrella of suspicion". John Ramsey later told CNN that the family were the prime suspects from the start: "They made up their mind day one."

The police held their first formal interviews with the couple on 30 April 1997, and in January 1998 the parents declined a second interview unless detectives let them review evidence, according to CNN's timeline. John Ramsey told the CBS programme 48 Hours in 2006 that the family should have told investigators from the beginning to charge them or clear them.

Not everyone working the case agreed with the focus on the family. Law Week Colorado, quoting court records, reported that Lou Smit, an experienced homicide detective retained by Boulder police in 1997, resigned in September 1998 because he felt the department refused to investigate leads pointing to an intruder. The same source says that Boulder police and the state's investigation bureau suspected Patsy Ramsey had staged the note, though no firm conclusion was reached. In 2003 a federal court in a defamation case in Atlanta ruled that Patsy Ramsey was highly unlikely to have written it. CBS News reported that the judge in that case said the evidence was more consistent with an intruder, and that Mary Lacy, by then the local district attorney, said she agreed.

Paula Woodward, a reporter who has covered the story from the start and wrote a book about it, said in a 2016 interview that law enforcement leaked false information to the press, for example that Patsy Ramsey had never given a DNA sample, and that her book was meant to correct inaccuracies. She told WPTV she did not know who killed JonBenét.
content.h2: The grand jury that charged and the prosecutor who refused
content.p: A Boulder grand jury of eight women and four men met for 13 months, hearing from dozens of witnesses and examining 30,000 pieces of evidence, according to CNN. They went home in October 1999, sworn to silence. On 13 October 1999 Hunter announced that there would be no indictments because the evidence fell short.

It was not until 2013 that the public learned more. In January that year the Boulder Daily Camera, citing unnamed jurors and an assistant district attorney, reported that the grand jury had in fact voted to indict. The newspaper and the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press sued, and Judge J. Robert Lowenbach ordered four pages released. They were made public on Friday 25 October 2013.

The pages showed that jurors had wanted to charge each parent with two counts: child abuse resulting in death, and acting as an accessory, meaning help given to an unnamed person so as to hinder that person's prosecution for first-degree murder and child abuse resulting in death. The documents did not say who that other person was. They described the offences as occurring between 25 and 26 December 1996. According to the Daily Camera, Hunter had not signed the indictment.

Opinions on what they meant diverged. The Ramseys' attorney, L. Lin Wood, called them "nonsensical" and said the jurors had not had the 2008 DNA results. CNN's legal analyst Jeffrey Toobin said the indictments showed only that a majority of grand jurors believed there was probable cause, a lower standard than proof beyond reasonable doubt, and that it was not clear what they thought the parents had done. Boulder police said that the documents showed the grand jury agreed with investigators that probable cause existed, while acknowledging that a trial would require a higher standard. The documents revealed little about the evidence the jurors had weighed. The Associated Press quoted University of Denver law professor Nancy Leong as saying the public knew little more factually than in 1996.

The profile that shapes the case today surfaced early. CBS News reported that police found male DNA in a drop of blood on JonBenét's underwear and that it did not come from anyone in her family. Prosecutors could not say whose it was or whether the person was the killer. Late in the year before the letter, the district attorney's office sent the long johns she had been wearing to Bode Technology Group, near Washington, to look for "touch DNA", the cells left behind where someone has handled an object. Bode developed a profile from the two sides of the long johns, where, authorities said, an attacker would have grasped the clothing, and it matched the earlier profile.

On 9 July 2008 Lacy wrote to John Ramsey. The letter said that the match of male DNA on two separate items of clothing made it "clear to us that an unknown male handled these items", and that the office did not consider his immediate family, including his wife Patsy and son Burke, to be under any suspicion. "To the extent that we may have contributed in any way to the public perception that you might have been involved in this crime, I am deeply sorry," she wrote. She said the office would treat the Ramseys as the victims of the crime. Her office's position, she said in a statement, was that the profile belonged to the perpetrator of the homicide.

Lacy did not claim the DNA alone would solve the case. Her letter said that its resolution would depend on more than matching DNA, and that the office hoped for a hit in the national CODIS database. Patsy Ramsey had died of ovarian cancer on 24 June 2006, aged 49; Lacy wrote that she wished the office could have cleared the family before then. Westword reported that online forums were sceptical about how much the DNA showed, and one poster questioned how many genetic markers the touch DNA contained. WPTV reported in 2016 that an investigation by the Daily Camera and the television station KUSA, which the two news organizations said uncovered flaws in how earlier DNA results had been interpreted, which prompted talk of new testing.

In August 2006 officials announced the arrest in Bangkok of John Mark Karr, a 41-year-old sometime teacher who had made a confession by email. Prosecutors dropped the case after DNA testing did not link him to the crime. Over the years the Ramseys and others filed and settled several defamation suits. Burke Ramsey sued CBS, a production company and the pathologist Dr. Werner Spitz for $250 million in December 2016 after a CBS docu-series suggested he might have been responsible; Michigan court documents show it was dismissed on 2 January 2019 after an undisclosed settlement. Another action by John Ramsey against CBS appears to have been settled the same day.
content.h2: The police and the push for new technology
content.p: Jurisdiction has moved over the years. Boulder police resumed their status as lead agency in February 2009, having been displaced when the district attorney's office took responsibility for the investigation in 2002. In 2016 District Attorney Stan Garnett said the Colorado Bureau of Investigation would test certain evidence, including possibly the duct tape, wrist ligatures, part of the garrote and a flashlight, with a Y-chromosome test. He did not expect "dramatic developments". The last earlier DNA test, on the wrist ligatures in autumn 2008, had been inconclusive.

In December 2021 Boulder police said they had processed more than 1,500 pieces of evidence and analysed nearly 1,000 DNA samples, 750 of them reference samples through the CBI. The DNA, they said, matched none of the persons of interest, and the profiles had not found a hit in CODIS. The Gazette quoted John Andrew Ramsey, JonBenét's half-brother, as saying "What the Boulder police have done to date is not enough." In 2022 John Ramsey backed an online petition asking Colorado's governor to hand DNA decisions to an outside agency; a spokesperson for Governor Jared Polis said the state would review it and consider how it could help with new technology. In November 2022 the police and District Attorney Michael Dougherty announced a consultation with the Colorado Cold Case Review Team and a private DNA laboratory, and warned that the DNA available was "extremely small and complex" and might be consumed by testing.

Under Chief Stephen Redfearn, John Ramsey's public stance toward the police shifted. After meeting police in late January 2025, John Ramsey told CNN he was "very satisfied and impressed with the leadership now in place". He said he wanted investigative genetic genealogy, a technique that links DNA to relatives through family trees, and called it "the only way this case will be solved". Redfearn said in a November statement that the claim that viable evidence and leads were not being pursued, including DNA testing, was "completely false". In December 2025 Fox News reported that Redfearn said in a video statement that the investigation "remains a top priority".

John Ramsey has given interviews arguing for particular steps. He told the Daily Mail, as reported by Fox News, that he believed there was a 70 percent chance the killer could be named within months, and he named the garrote as the evidence he most wanted tested or retested. He also pointed to a list of potential persons of interest compiled by Smit, which he said was 700 people long; Fox News, citing the Daily Mail, said Smit theorised the killer held a grudge against Ramsey. These are Ramsey's views and Smit's theory, not findings by police. Police say they have followed up on "every lead".

The department's latest public statements invite information from anyone who knows anything. Redfearn said in December 2025: "It is never too late for people with knowledge of this terrible crime to come forward."
